BASICMED AIRCRAFT LIMITS (14 CFR 61.113(i)(1), as in force)

1) Maximum takeoff weight: 12,500 pounds (maximum certificated takeoff weight, MTOW — not actual weight at the time of flight).
2) Maximum authorized occupants: 7 occupants — i.e., the aircraft's design approval must authorize no more than seven occupants, counting the pilot and any required flightcrew.
3) Maximum passengers on board: 6 passengers.

Additional condition in the same paragraph: the aircraft may not be a transport category rotorcraft certified to airworthiness standards under 14 CFR part 29.

AUTHORITATIVE TEXT (quoted from 14 CFR 61.113(i)(1), eCFR current):
"The aircraft is authorized to carry not more than 7 occupants, has a maximum takeoff weight of not more than 12,500 pounds, is operated with no more than 6 passengers on board, and is not a transport category rotorcraft certified to airworthiness standards under part 29 of this chapter."

EFFECTIVE DATE AND PROVENANCE
The three limits above are the post-expansion figures, effective on or after November 12, 2024, per PL 118-63 (FAA Reauthorization Act of 2024) Sec. 828, "Expansion of BasicMed," implemented by FAA final rule (Amdt. 61-158, 89 FR 90577, Nov. 18, 2024). FAA Notice N 8000.386 (11/14/24) states the same triad and dates it: "the following aircraft limitations will apply on or after November 12, 2024: the aircraft is authorized to carry no more than seven occupants, the aircraft has an MTOW of no more than 12,500 pounds, and the aircraft is operated with no more than six passengers on board." The FAA newsroom release "FAA Updates BasicMed Program" (Nov. 15, 2024) confirms: "Increase the number of allowable passengers to six from five, and the number of occupants to seven from six. Increase the maximum aircraft takeoff weight to 12,500 lbs. from 6,000 lbs., excluding transport category helicopters." The eCFR amendment history for 61.113 runs through Amdt. 61-159 (90 FR 35218, July 24, 2025), confirming the paragraph is current.

SUPERSEDED FIGURES — DO NOT USE
Pre-November 12, 2024 BasicMed was: 6 occupants, 6,000 lb MTOW, 5 passengers. Those numbers appear in the 2024 printed CFR (CFR-2024-title14-vol2, sec. 61.113) and in FAA Advisory Circular AC 68-1A (5/3/17), Chapter 5. AC 68-1A predates the expansion and its Chapter 5 figures are stale; where AC 68-1A and the current regulation differ, the current regulation controls. Anyone using AC 68-1A as a checklist must substitute 7 / 12,500 / 6.

HOW THE THREE NUMBERS FIT TOGETHER (so the answer is internally consistent)
- "Occupants" is a certification/authorization property of the aircraft: the count the design approval (TC, STC, or amended TC) permits, per AC 68-1A 5.1.2. It is not the number of people actually aboard.
- "Passengers" is an operational limit on a given flight. Passengers = occupants aboard minus the pilot(s).
- With one pilot: 1 pilot + 6 passengers = 7 occupants — the passenger cap and occupant cap bind simultaneously, so the limits are consistent with no gap or overlap.
- If the aircraft is type certificated for two pilot flightcrew members, 2 flightcrew + 5 additional occupants = 7 occupants; the passenger limit still caps the flight at 6 passengers, and the binding constraint in that case is the occupant count.
- The weight limit is a ceiling on certificated MTOW, so no compliant aircraft can exceed it; it is a qualification test on the aircraft, not a weight-and-balance computation for the flight.
- The aircraft must still be operated within its own operating limitations; 61.113(i)(1) does not relieve the aircraft of its operating limitations, and if those conflict with the BasicMed limits, the operating limitations govern (AC 68-1A 5.1.1).

CAVEATS TO CARRY FORWARD
- Out of scope per the request but adjacent: the BasicMed flight limits (at or below 18,000 ft MSL; within the U.S. or a country authorizing BasicMed; indicated airspeed not exceeding 250 knots) and the logbook carriage requirements (completed CMEC under 68.7 and course completion certificate under 61.23(c)(3)).
- Experimental aircraft: AC 68-1A points to 14 CFR 91.319(j) as a separate occupant cap for experimental aircraft operated under BasicMed. That cross-reference should be re-verified against the current 91.319 text, since AC 68-1A predates the expansion; do not assume the AC's stated figure survives unchanged.
- A pilot operating under BasicMed still may not act as PIC for compensation or hire (61.113(a)), which is unaffected by these aircraft limits.

SCOPE AND CONTROLLING RULE

Assumption: the driver operates a passenger-carrying commercial motor vehicle (CMV), such as a motorcoach, in interstate commerce in the contiguous United States, and no exception or exemption in 49 CFR 395.1 applies (including no short-haul, adverse-driving, emergency, Alaska, or Hawaii special provision). Under those assumptions, the controlling federal rule is 49 CFR 395.5, Maximum driving time for passenger-carrying vehicles.

49 CFR 395.5 provides, in relevant part:

- 395.5(a)(1): no motor carrier may permit or require a driver of a passenger-carrying CMV, and no such driver may drive, more than 10 hours following 8 consecutive hours off duty.
- 395.5(a)(2): no such driver may drive for any period after having been on duty 15 hours following 8 consecutive hours off duty.
- 395.5(b): no such driver may drive after having been on duty 60 hours in any 7 consecutive days if the employing motor carrier does not operate CMVs every day of the week, or after having been on duty 70 hours in any period of 8 consecutive days if the employing motor carrier operates CMVs every day of the week.

The rule is expressly subject to the exceptions and exemptions in 49 CFR 395.1.

ANSWERS

1. Maximum driving time: 10 hours. A passenger-carrying CMV driver may drive no more than 10 hours following 8 consecutive hours off duty.

2. Required consecutive off-duty period: 8 hours. Before driving, the driver must have at least 8 consecutive hours off duty. The property-carrying rule's 10-hour off-duty requirement does not apply to this passenger-carrying operation.

3. On-duty threshold after which driving is prohibited: 15 hours. The driver may not drive after having been on duty 15 hours following 8 consecutive hours off duty. This is an on-duty limit, not a 15-hour driving allowance; driving remains separately capped at 10 hours.

COMPLIANCE PROCEDURE

Step 1. Confirm the driver had at least 8 consecutive hours off duty before starting the duty period. Do not start driving without that 8-hour consecutive off-duty break.

Step 2. Start counting driving time and on-duty time from the end of that 8-hour off-duty period.

Step 3. Stop driving when either limit is reached first:
- driving time reaches 10 hours; or
- on-duty time reaches 15 hours.

Step 4. The 15-hour limit includes driving time plus all other on-duty time, such as inspections, loading or unloading, dispatching, passenger assistance, paperwork, and waiting time that is on duty rather than off duty. A driver who has been on duty 15 hours may not drive, even if the driver has accumulated fewer than 10 driving hours.

Step 5. Before dispatch, also check the applicable weekly limit: 60 on-duty hours in 7 consecutive days if the carrier does not operate CMVs every day of the week, or 70 on-duty hours in 8 consecutive days if the carrier operates CMVs every day of the week. These weekly limits are context only and do not change the three requested daily-cycle values.

DEFINITIONS AND COUNTING NOTES

Use the 49 CFR 395.2 definitions for driving time, on-duty time, and off-duty time. In general terms, driving time is time spent at the controls of a CMV in operation; on-duty time includes driving plus other work or required availability; off-duty time is time relieved of all duty. For passenger-carrying operations, FMCSA guidance also notes that time spent working at another job of any kind must be included as on-duty time.

LIMITS OF THIS ANSWER

This answer states the federal interstate passenger-carrying limits. If the operation is purely intrastate, state hours-of-service rules may differ and must be checked separately. If any 49 CFR 395.1 exception or exemption applies, including short-haul, adverse driving conditions, emergency relief, or the special Alaska or Hawaii provisions, the numeric limits may differ. None of those exceptions is assumed here.

# Flight Attendant Rest After a Scheduled Duty Period of 14 Hours or Less — 14 CFR Part 135

## 1. Direct answer

| # | Question | Answer | Authority |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Rest required after a scheduled duty period of 14 hours or less | **At least 9 consecutive hours** of scheduled rest | § 135.273(b)(2) |
| 2 | Extent to which that rest may be reduced | **To 8 consecutive hours** (never less), and only if a subsequent rest of **at least 10 consecutive hours** is scheduled to begin **no later than 24 hours after the beginning of the reduced rest period** | § 135.273(b)(3) |

Both rest periods must fall between the completion of the scheduled duty period and the commencement of the subsequent duty period.

## 2. Why this section governs

- § 135.261(e): "Section 135.273 prescribes duty period limitations and rest requirements for flight attendants in all operations conducted under this part." Part 135 flight-attendant rest is therefore governed by § 135.273 regardless of whether the operation is on-demand or scheduled, and regardless of aircraft type.
- § 135.273(b) opens: "a certificate holder may assign a duty period to a flight attendant only when the applicable duty period limitations and rest requirements of this paragraph are met."
- § 135.273(a) defines the operative term: "Rest period means the period free of all responsibility for work or duty should the occasion arise."
- The flight-crewmember rest tables in §§ 135.265, 135.267 and 135.269 (9/10/11 hours, 10 hours, and the 8/11/12-hour reduction floors) do **not** apply to a flight attendant unless the certificate holder makes the election described in § 6 below.

## 3. The governing text

**§ 135.273(b)(1)** — the 14-hour baseline:
> "Except as provided in paragraphs (b)(4), (b)(5), and (b)(6) of this section, no certificate holder may assign a flight attendant to a scheduled duty period of more than 14 hours."

**§ 135.273(b)(2)** — the 9-hour answer:
> "Except as provided in paragraph (b)(3) of this section, a flight attendant scheduled to a duty period of 14 hours or less as provided under paragraph (b)(1) of this section must be given a scheduled rest period of at least 9 consecutive hours. This rest period must occur between the completion of the scheduled duty period and the commencement of the subsequent duty period."

**§ 135.273(b)(3)** — the 8-hour answer and its conditions:
> "The rest period required under paragraph (b)(2) of this section may be scheduled or reduced to 8 consecutive hours if the flight attendant is provided a subsequent rest period of at least 10 consecutive hours; this subsequent rest period must be scheduled to begin no later than 24 hours after the beginning of the reduced rest period and must occur between the completion of the scheduled duty period and the commencement of the subsequent duty period."

**Enforcement backstops:**
- § 135.273(b)(10): "No certificate holder may assign a flight attendant any duty period with the certificate holder unless the flight attendant has had at least the minimum rest required under this section."
- § 135.273(b)(11): "No certificate holder may assign a flight attendant to perform any duty with the certificate holder during any required rest period."

## 4. Conditions on the 8-hour reduction — all four must hold

The reduction in (b)(3) is conditional, not discretionary in the abstract. Before a scheduler may use 8 hours, all of the following must be true on the schedule:

1. **Floor.** The reduced rest is **8 consecutive hours** — it may not be 7:59 or less. There is no provision in Part 135 permitting a flight attendant's post-duty rest to fall below 8 consecutive hours for a duty period of 14 hours or less.
2. **Compensatory rest.** A **subsequent rest period of at least 10 consecutive hours** is scheduled.
3. **Timing.** That subsequent rest period is **scheduled to begin no later than 24 hours after the beginning of the reduced rest period**. The clock starts at the *beginning* of the reduced rest, not at its end and not at the end of the intervening duty period. The subsequent rest may *end* after the 24-hour mark; only its *start* is bounded.
4. **Placement.** The subsequent rest must occur **between the completion of the scheduled duty period** (i.e., the duty period that followed the reduced rest) **and the commencement of the subsequent duty period**.

Sequence implied by (b)(3):

```
Duty A ends
  └─ reduced rest, 8 h minimum, begins at T
       └─ Duty B  (must be completed by T + 24 h)
            └─ subsequent rest, 10 h minimum, begins at T + 24 h or earlier
                 └─ Duty C
```

Note what (b)(3) does **not** contain: unlike the augmented-crew reduction in (b)(8)–(b)(9), the (b)(3) reduction carries no express cap on the length of the intervening duty period. Duty B remains independently limited by § 135.273(b)(1) (not more than 14 hours scheduled, absent augmentation under (b)(4)–(b)(6)) and by any operations-specification or manual limitation.

## 5. Worked timelines

Assume all times local at the rest station, and that the flight attendant is free of all responsibility for work or duty during the rest period.

**Example A — full 9 hours (no reduction).**
- Duty A completes Monday 21:00.
- 9 consecutive hours → earliest permissible start of the next duty period: **Tuesday 06:00**.

**Example B — 8-hour reduction with compliant compensatory rest.**
- Duty A completes Monday 21:00. Reduced rest begins **T = Monday 21:00**.
- 8 consecutive hours → Duty B may begin Tuesday 05:00.
- 24-hour limit for the start of the subsequent rest: **T + 24 = Tuesday 21:00**. Duty B must therefore be completed no later than Tuesday 21:00.
- If Duty B completes Tuesday 19:00, the subsequent rest begins 19:00 Tuesday (before the T+24 limit — compliant) and must run at least 10 consecutive hours, to **Wednesday 05:00**. The fact that this rest *ends* after T+24 is irrelevant; the regulation bounds only when it *begins*.
- Duty C may begin no earlier than Wednesday 05:00.

**Example C — reduction unavailable.**
- Duty A completes Monday 21:00; the schedule requires the flight attendant back on duty Tuesday 05:00 (8 hours) and shows no duty-free block of at least 10 consecutive hours beginning by Tuesday 21:00.
- The 8-hour reduction is **not** available. The only lawful options are to move the Tuesday report time to 06:00 or later (9 hours) or to rebuild the pairing so the compensatory rest exists.

## 6. The one fact that would change the answer — § 135.273(c) election

§ 135.273(c) permits a certificate holder, notwithstanding paragraph (b), to apply the **flight crewmember** flight time and duty limitations and rest requirements of Part 135 to flight attendants for all operations under Part 135, provided it establishes written procedures that:
- apply to all flight attendants used in the operation;
- include the subpart F flight crewmember requirements as appropriate to the operation (rest facilities on board are not required);
- add one flight attendant to the minimum complement for each flight crewmember above the minimum required by the aircraft type certificate data sheet; and
- are **approved by the Administrator and described or referenced in the certificate holder's operations specifications**.

If — and only if — such an approved election is in place, the rest baseline shifts to the flight-crewmember rule (for on-demand operations, § 135.267(d): at least 10 consecutive hours of rest in the 24 hours preceding planned completion of the assignment), and the corresponding flight-crewmember reduction provisions apply. **Absent an approved operations-specification election, the answer remains 9 hours, reducible to 8.** The requesting operator should confirm its ops specs contain no such election; the assumption in this answer is that none does.

Other facts that would tighten (never loosen) the answer:
- A collective bargaining agreement or company manual provision more restrictive than the regulation — the more restrictive term controls as a matter of the operator's own obligation.
- Any operations-specification or manual rest provision more restrictive than § 135.273.
- The same individual also serving as a flight crewmember on the flight — that flight is then governed by the flight-crewmember rest rules of subpart F in addition.

## 7. Compliance procedure for the scheduler / crew records

1. **Compute from the scheduled duty period, not the actual one.** The trigger in (b)(1)–(b)(2) is the *scheduled* duty period. Build the rest block from the scheduled completion time.
2. **Default to 9 hours.** Use 8 hours only through a documented reduction decision.
3. **Reduction checklist before publishing a pairing:** (a) reduced rest ≥ 8:00 consecutive; (b) a named subsequent rest block ≥ 10:00 consecutive exists; (c) that block begins no later than the reduced-rest start time + 24:00; (d) that block sits between the end of the intervening duty period and the start of the following duty period.
4. **Record the rest block** in the crew scheduling/duty-time system consistent with the certificate holder's recordkeeping obligations under § 135.63 and its manual, including which basis (9-hour or 8-hour reduction) was used and the start/end times of both rest blocks when the reduction is used.
5. **Do not assign any duty during required rest** — including deadheading, positioning, training, administrative work, or being on call in a status that constitutes responsibility for work or duty (§ 135.273(b)(11), and the (a) definition of rest period).
6. **Verify at assignment:** no duty period may be assigned unless the flight attendant has actually had at least the minimum rest (§ 135.273(b)(10)); an actual shortfall is a violation even if the schedule was lawful.

## 8. Common errors this answer is written to prevent

- Using **10 hours** as the Part 135 flight-attendant baseline. Ten hours is the flight-crewmember figure (§ 135.267(d)) or the augmented-crew reduced figure (§ 135.273(b)(8)); it is not the (b)(2) answer.
- Using **8 hours** as an unconditional entitlement. Eight hours exists only inside the (b)(3) condition set.
- Measuring the 24-hour window from the *end* of the reduced rest or from the end of the intervening duty period instead of from the **beginning** of the reduced rest.
- Assuming the (b)(9) 14-hour intervening-duty cap applies to the (b)(3) reduction. It does not; (b)(9) is expressly tied to the (b)(8) reduction.
- Importing Part 121 rest figures (e.g., § 121.467) into a Part 135 operation.

## 9. Bottom line for the operator

Give the flight attendant **at least 9 consecutive hours** of rest, free of all duty, between the completion of a scheduled duty period of 14 hours or less and the start of the next duty period. That rest may be **reduced to 8 consecutive hours** only if a **subsequent rest of at least 10 consecutive hours** is scheduled to begin **no later than 24 hours after the reduced rest began**, and both rest blocks fall between the duty periods they separate. Nothing in Part 135 permits less than 8 consecutive hours in this situation.

2. **National Minimum Wage, 18 to 20 year olds: £10.85 per hour** (the "18–20 Year Old Rate" applicable from 1 April 2026).

## Effective date and status

- Both rates took effect on **1 April 2026**. Statutory minimum wage rates change on 1 April each year; there is no mid-year variation.
- The figures are **final and in force**, not proposals. The Low Pay Commission recommended them in advice submitted on 27 October 2025 (published 26 November 2025); the Government accepted the recommendations in full at the Autumn Budget on 26 November 2025; the rates came into force on 1 April 2026.
- Because the source pages were retrieved on 16 November 2026, the April 2026 figures above are also the rates **currently in force** at the time of writing. The request's ambiguity over whether the 18–20 figure meant "April 2026" or "current" therefore has no practical effect: both readings give £10.85.

## Definitions and scope

- **"National Living Wage" here means the UK Government's statutory NLW** — the top band of the National Minimum Wage, payable to workers aged 21 and over. It is **not** the Living Wage Foundation's voluntary "Real Living Wage", which is a separate, higher, independently calculated figure with a different (UK-wide and London) update cycle and no statutory force. If the Real Living Wage was intended, this answer does not cover it.
- The NLW age threshold has moved: 25+ before April 2021, 23+ from April 2021, and **21+ from April 2024** — the threshold applying throughout the April 2026 rate year.
- Workers aged 20 and under are not entitled to the NLW; the relevant NMW youth rate applies instead. A 21-year-old is on the NLW rate from their 21st birthday, not from the following April.
- **Apprentices:** entitled to the £8.00 apprentice rate if aged under 19, or aged 19+ and in the first year of their apprenticeship. An apprentice aged 19+ who has completed the first year moves onto the rate for their age (e.g. £12.71 for a 21-year-old).
- All figures are **gross hourly pay in pounds sterling**, before tax and National Insurance, as published by the UK Government. They are UK-wide; there is no regional variation in the statutory rates.

## Notes for a payroll user

- Rates apply pro rata to the pay reference period; salaried hours, time work, output work and unmeasured work each have their own compliance calculation.
- Deductions and required employer-provided accommodation can reduce the amount payable only within the accommodation offset (£11.10 for April 2026) — the offset is not an addition to the wage.
- Records proving payment at or above these rates must be kept for six years (three years in Northern Ireland).

COMPLIANCE DETERMINATION — FMCSA SHORT-HAUL EXCEPTION (§ 395.1(e)(1))

BOTTOM LINE
1. Radius: the driver must operate within a 150 air-mile radius of the normal work reporting location (150 air-miles = 172.6 statute miles, as the regulation itself states). Air miles are straight-line miles, not highway miles.
2. Release: the driver must return to the work reporting location and be released from work within 14 consecutive hours.

CONTROLLING TEXT — 49 CFR § 395.1(e)(1), 'Short-haul operations — 150 air-mile radius driver' (eCFR, current):
"(e) Short-haul operations — (1) 150 air-mile radius driver. A driver is exempt from the requirements of §§ 395.8 and 395.11 if: (i) The driver operates within a 150 air-mile radius (172.6 statute miles) of the normal work reporting location; (ii) The driver, except a driver-salesperson, returns to the work reporting location and is released from work within 14 consecutive hours; (iii) (A) A property-carrying commercial motor vehicle driver has at least 10 consecutive hours off-duty separating each 14 hours on-duty; (B) A passenger-carrying commercial motor vehicle driver has at least 8 consecutive hours off-duty separating each 14 hours on-duty; and (iv) The motor carrier that employs the driver maintains and retains for a period of 6 months accurate and true time records showing: (A) The time the driver reports for duty each day; (B) The total number of hours the driver is on-duty each day; (C) The time the driver is released from duty each day; and (D) The total time for the preceding 7 days in accordance with § 395.8(j)(2) for drivers used for the first time or intermittently."

CORROBORATION (all consistent with 150 / 14):
- FMCSA, Summary of Hours of Service Regulations: "A driver is exempt from the requirements of §395.8 and §395.11 if: the driver operates within a 150 air-mile radius of the normal work reporting location, and the driver does not exceed a maximum duty period of 14 hours. Drivers using the short-haul exception in §395.1(e)(1) must report and return to the normal work reporting location within 14 consecutive hours, and stay within a 150 air-mile radius of the work reporting location."
- FMCSA, Hours of Service Drivers Final Rule fact sheet: "Extends the maximum duty period allowed under the short-haul exception from 12 hours to 14 hours. Extends the maximum radius of the short-haul exception from a 100 air-mile radius to a 150 air-mile radius."
- FMCSA HOS Visor Card: "A driver is exempt from the requirements of § 395.8 and § 395.11 if: the driver operates within a 150 air-mile radius of the normal work reporting location, and the driver does not exceed a maximum duty period of 14 hours."

HOW TO APPLY IT (compliance operating rules)
- Measure from the normal work reporting location — the fixed location where the driver reports to and is released from work. Measure the 150 air miles as a straight-line radius from that point to every point the vehicle reaches during the duty tour; the radius is a boundary on the driver's operating area, not on the route distance driven.
- The 14-hour clock runs from the time the driver comes on duty. The exception is satisfied only if the driver is back at the work reporting location and released from work by hour 14. It is not enough to stop driving by hour 14; the return and the release must both occur inside the 14 consecutive hours.
- The 14-hour condition does not apply to a driver-salesperson (the 'except a driver-salesperson' clause in (e)(1)(ii)); the radius condition still does.
- Even with the exception, the driver remains subject to the underlying driving and on-duty limits of § 395.3 (11-hour driving limit, 60/70-hour limit); the exception relieves only §§ 395.8 (RODS) and 395.11 (supporting documents). FMCSA guidance further states that property and passenger carriers qualifying under § 395.1(e)(1) are not required to use a RODS or ELD, or to take the 30-minute break.
- The carrier must still keep accurate and true time records for 6 months showing report-for-duty time, total on-duty hours, release-from-duty time each day, and the preceding-7-day total for newly used or intermittent drivers.

FAILURE MODE
If on a given day the driver leaves the 150 air-mile radius, or is not returned and released within 14 consecutive hours, the exception is not available for that day and the driver must complete a record of duty status for that day under § 395.8 (and use an ELD if § 395.8(a)/part 395 subpart B otherwise requires it), unless a different exemption applies. The exception is applied day by day; a failed day does not retroactively invalidate compliant days.

DO NOT CONFUSE WITH ADJACENT PROVISIONS (these are not the answer to either ask)
- § 395.1(e)(2) (non-CDL 150 air-mile driver): same 150 air-mile radius, but the time condition is expressed as not driving after the 14th hour on 5 days of any 7 and after the 16th hour on 2 days of any 7, plus return to the normal work reporting location at the end of each duty tour — not a 'released within 14 consecutive hours' rule.
- § 395.1(o) (16-hour exception): release within 16 hours after coming on duty, after returning to the normal work reporting location for the previous 5 duty tours, and not used within the previous 6 consecutive days. The number 16 belongs here, not to the short-haul exception.
- § 395.1(p) (motion picture production sites): 100 air-mile radius. The number 100 is the pre-2020 short-haul radius and the current motion-picture radius; it is not the current short-haul radius.

BASIS AND LIMITS OF THIS ANSWER
Grounded in the current eCFR text of 49 CFR § 395.1(e)(1) plus three FMCSA publications (Summary of HOS Regulations; HOS Drivers Final Rule fact sheet; HOS Visor Card), all of which agree on 150 air-miles and 14 hours. The answer covers US federal FMCSA hours-of-service rules for property- and passenger-carrying CMVs in interstate commerce. It does not address state intrastate rules, Canadian or Mexican rules, or sector-specific exemptions outside Part 395; if any of those govern the driver, the numeric thresholds must be re-verified against that authority before use.

Hours of Service Drivers Final Rule
FMCSA revises the hours of service (HOS) regulations to provide greater flexibility for drivers subject to those rules without adversely affecting safety. The Agency: (1) expands the short-haul exception to 150 air-miles and allows a 14-hour work shift to take place as part of the exception; (2) expands the driving window during adverse driving conditions by up to an additional 2 hours; (3) requires a 30-minute break after 8 hours of driving time (instead of on-duty time) and allows an on-duty/not driving period to qualify as the required break; and (4) modifies the sleeper berth exception to allow a driver to meet the 10-hour minimum off-duty requirement by spending at least 7, rather than at least 8 hours of that period in the berth and a minimum off-duty period of at least 2 hours spent inside or outside of the berth, provided the two periods total at least 10 hours, and that neither qualifying period counts against the 14-hour driving window.
